name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler

lead: PMMA filler is made of tiny plastic microspheres in a carrier gel, sold in the US as Artefill and Bellafill. It is injected for permanent volume in the cheeks and chin and to lift acne scars, so the result is visible straight away and stays.

The microspheres are not absorbed, so the body forms fibrous collagen tissue around them, which adds lasting volume. The FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars. PMMA is also the polymer in bone cement and dentures, and some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it for muscle shaping. Published cosmetic outcome data are limited to registered studies and reviews.

paras: It is placed by a clinician, usually in small amounts in stages. Looksmax forums mostly mention it in cautionary threads, for example when a surgeon offered PMMA bone cement for facial implants.

The FDA lists lumps, granulomas, infection, migration, permanent hard nodules and rare vascular injury including blindness as filler complications, some appearing years later. It says removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible. Use in the buttocks, muscles or other unapproved sites is not sanctioned.

chain: Lasting volume in chin, cheeks, scars
angle.text: PMMA filler (Artefill, Bellafill) places permanent microspheres in the cheeks, chin or acne scars, and the body builds collagen around them, so volume shows right away and stays. Published outcome data are limited, and bodybuilders have also injected PMMA-type products for muscle size.

lead: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler is a non-absorbable injectable made of tiny PMMA microspheres suspended in a carrier gel, sold in the United States under names such as Artefill and Bellafill. Because the microspheres are not broken down by the body, the fillers are described as permanent: the particles stay in place and prompt the body to form fibrous tissue around them [1][2][3].

The US FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and for acne scars of the cheek, and it states that removal can be difficult or impossible for permanent fillers. A review of jawline and chin fillers includes PMMA among the materials used in the lower face. PMMA is the same polymer used in bone cement, dentures and other implants, and some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it to shape muscles [3].

Published human evidence on cosmetic PMMA filler in the sources used here is limited to registered studies and reviews. Looksmaxxing forums discuss PMMA mostly as a cautionary subject, for example when a surgeon offered PMMA bone cement for facial implants.

paras: PMMA fillers consist of microscopic PMMA beads held in a gel. Rather than being degraded, the particulate scaffold stays in the tissue and provokes fibrous tissue formation around the beads, which supplies the volume [3]. Wikipedia describes the injected microspheres as a soft-tissue filler intended to reduce wrinkles or scars permanently [3].

The FDA states that non-absorbable fillers are approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and that unapproved uses include breast, buttock and foot enhancement and injection into the nose, forehead, periorbital area, neck or muscle. PMMA was also widely used in the early 2000s to restore volume in people with HIV-related facial wasting [3].

A 2023 review of fillers for the chin and jawline covers hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, poly-L-lactic acid and PMMA as options, noting that the advantages of fillers include relatively affordable cost and limited recovery time, and that measures are needed to prevent short- and long-term complications.

The FDA's general information on dermal fillers lists bruising, redness, swelling and pain as common; nodules or granulomas, infection and allergic reaction as less common; and filler migration, permanent hard nodules and vascular injury leading to tissue death, vision loss or stroke as rare. It adds that problems can appear weeks, months or years after injection. Because PMMA is not absorbed, any such complication is not self-limiting in the way it can be with temporary fillers, a point the FDA makes about permanent fillers generally.

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a post-approval study of Artefill for nasolabial folds enrolling 1,008 participants, begun in 2007, with granulomatous disorder as its listed condition [1]. A phase 1 study of Artefill for HIV-associated facial lipoatrophy (31 participants, 2013) is also registered [2]. Results from these registrations are not summarised in the sources used here.

Registered trials of PMMA for gluteal augmentation (one of 137 and one of 133 participants) are listed as not yet recruiting or of unknown status [4][5]; gluteal use is outside the FDA's list of approved filler uses. A 2016 review titled Synthetic Fillers for Facial Rejuvenation covers the category.

On looksmax.org, a user reported that his surgeon proposed PMMA bone cement for cheek (infraorbital/malar) implants as a cheaper alternative to PEEK or hydroxyapatite, saying it was biocompatible; the user had heard PMMA was dangerous and asked about side effects, and one reply simply advised against it. That thread concerns bone-cement implants rather than injectable microspheres.

On T Nation, members have said bodybuilder Rich Piana reportedly had PMMA in his arms, and another poster described fear of reduced function from synthol-type injections [6][7]. These are forum statements and are not verified by the sources used here.

lore.intro: PMMA is mentioned in forums mainly in connection with implants and muscle-shaping injections, usually with caution rather than endorsement [6][7].
